---
title: "Stochastic volatility"
subtitle: "Lecture 12"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can treat an asset's variance as a hidden random
process rather than a constant or a deterministic function of the past, and turn a
likelihood that has no closed form into a posterior you can actually sample.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For a stochastic-volatility model $r_t = \exp(h_t/2)\,u_t$, $h_t = \mu +
\phi(h_{t-1}-\mu) + \sigma_h\zeta_t$, with $u_t,\zeta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$
independent of each other and over time, the posterior of the latent path
$h_{1:T}$ together with $(\mu,\phi,\sigma_h)$ can be sampled one date, or one
block, at a time even though the likelihood

$$
p(r_{1:T}\mid\mu,\phi,\sigma_h)
= \int p(r_{1:T}\mid h_{1:T})\, p(h_{1:T}\mid \mu,\phi,\sigma_h)\,\mathrm{d}h_{1:T}
$$

has no closed form. Each full conditional of a single state is Gaussian in its
neighbours and non-Gaussian only through the single return observed that day,
which is enough structure for an exact Metropolis step. The difficulty is that
neighbouring states are strongly dependent whenever volatility is persistent, so
the chain that recovers them mixes slowly.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why a nonlinear measurement equation breaks the Kalman recursion and
   leaves the likelihood as an intractable integral;
2. derive the full conditional of a single log-volatility as a Gaussian
   neighbour term combined with a non-Gaussian likelihood correction;
3. derive an accept-reject and Metropolis construction that draws exactly from
   that full conditional using a moment-matched inverse-gamma proposal;
4. implement a single-move Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler for a
   stochastic-volatility model in Python;
5. interpret the estimated persistence, volatility of volatility, and posterior
   volatility path of a real return series;
6. compare a Bayesian stochastic-volatility estimate with an industry-standard
   exponentially weighted variance and say what each does and does not deliver;
7. diagnose why persistence and volatility of volatility are only weakly
   separated in the posterior even with a long sample.

Week 12 of 15, paired with the [Week 12 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/12-stochastic-volatility.qmd). The chapter assumes
the state-space machinery and the Kalman filter of Lecture 8 and the
Metropolis-Hastings construction of Lecture 5; the model-averaging of Lecture 9
is not needed.

## Motivation: every earlier model priced risk with a variance that never moves {#sec-motivation}

Every regression, every vector autoregression and every state-space model built so
far in this course writes the shock in its measurement equation as
$\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ or $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$, a single
number or a single matrix standing for risk over the whole estimation window.
Lecture 8 let the coefficients drift through time, but even there the innovation
variance of every equation was held fixed, because a constant variance is exactly
what keeps the Kalman filter available. A risk manager who sized a position with
any of these models would be using the same variance on a quiet Tuesday in 2017
and on the Monday a pandemic was declared.

Whether that assumption is defensible is a question about data rather than
taste, and daily returns settle it quickly. A risk desk sizing a position for
tomorrow needs an estimate of tomorrow's variance, not last decade's average one,
and every model built in this course so far would hand it the same number
regardless of whether the last month looked like early 2017 or March 2020.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

ff_d = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_daily.parquet")
window = ff_d["2005-01-01":"2022-12-31"]
dates = window.index
r = (window["mkt_rf"] - window["mkt_rf"].mean()).to_numpy()
T = r.size

roll_vol = pd.Series(r, index=dates).rolling(21).std() * np.sqrt(252)

def acf(x, lag):
    x = x - x.mean()
    return np.corrcoef(x[:-lag], x[lag:])[0, 1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(dates, roll_vol, color="steelblue", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("21-day rolling annualised volatility"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("A single constant variance describes none of this")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{T} trading days, {dates[0]:%Y-%m-%d} to {dates[-1]:%Y-%m-%d}")
print(f"whole-sample annualised volatility {r.std(ddof=1)*np.sqrt(252):.2%}")
print(f"21-day rolling volatility: min {roll_vol.min():.2%}, max {roll_vol.max():.2%}")
for lag in (1, 5, 20):
    print(f"lag {lag:2d}: return autocorrelation {acf(r, lag):+.3f}, "
          f"squared-return autocorrelation {acf(r**2, lag):+.3f}")
```

The rolling window is a moving picture of exactly the number every model so far has
held fixed, and it is not fixed at all: annualised volatility measured over
successive months ranges from $3.94\%$ to $96.64\%$, a factor of about twenty-five,
against a single whole-sample figure of $19.95\%$ that no month actually
experiences. The autocorrelation table says the same thing more precisely. The
return itself is close to unpredictable, with an autocorrelation of $-0.113$ at
one day and $0.017$ at twenty, the mild pattern classical market efficiency
predicts. Its square tells a different story: an autocorrelation of $0.332$ at one
day that is still $0.176$ a full trading month later. A large squared return today
makes a large squared return likely for weeks, even though the sign of the return
carries almost no memory at all.

A model with a single $\sigma^2$ cannot represent any of this, because it has
nowhere for the clustering to live. The traditional response, the GARCH family, keeps
the variance a deterministic function of past squared returns, so that once the
data are observed the whole variance path is known with certainty; that choice is
defensible and widely used, but it treats a variance estimated with noise as if it
were known exactly, the same overconfidence a plug-in point estimate always
carries. This chapter takes a different route, treating the variance as a
genuinely random, unobserved state with a shock of its own,
$h_t = \log(\text{variance}_t)$ evolving as an autoregression exactly like the
states of Lecture 8, so that the model itself carries an honest statement of how
uncertain today's variance is, not only its best guess.

That single change, a random rather than a deterministic state, is what breaks
every piece of machinery this course has built so far. Lecture 8 could compute the
posterior of a drifting coefficient in closed form at every date because the
Kalman filter turns a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian measurement into a Gaussian
posterior, one step at a time. The measurement equation here, $r_t =
\exp(h_t/2)u_t$, makes the variance itself the hidden state, and multiplying a
return by $\exp(h_t/2)$ rather than adding a state to it is exactly the change that
takes the Kalman recursion away, which the next section makes precise.

## The problem: a nonlinear measurement equation breaks the Kalman recursion {#sec-problem}

### Result R-12.1: the likelihood has no closed form

For $r_t = \exp(h_t/2)\,u_t$ with $h_t = \mu + \phi(h_{t-1}-\mu) + \sigma_h\zeta_t$
and $u_t,\zeta_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, the likelihood of
$\theta = (\mu,\phi,\sigma_h)$ requires integrating the entire latent path out of
the joint density,

$$
p(r_{1:T} \mid \theta)
= \int \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(r_t \mid h_t)\; p(h_{1:T} \mid \theta)\; \mathrm{d}h_{1:T},
\qquad p(r_t \mid h_t) = \mathcal{N}(0, e^{h_t}),
$$

an integral of dimension $T$ with no closed form for any $T > 1$. In a linear
Gaussian state-space model the Kalman filter computes exactly this integral
recursively, because each step multiplies a Gaussian prior over the state by a
measurement density that is Gaussian in the state, and the product of two
Gaussians is again Gaussian. Here the measurement density is Gaussian in $r_t$ but
its log kernel is not quadratic in $h_t$, so the recursion that every model in this
course has relied on so far cannot close.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: why the measurement density will not sit still for a Kalman update

Write the log measurement kernel as $\ell(h_t) = -h_t/2 - r_t^2 e^{-h_t}/2$. Its
first derivative is $\ell'(h_t) = \big[-1 + r_t^2 e^{-h_t}\big]/2$ and its second
derivative is $\ell''(h_t) = -r_t^2 e^{-h_t}/2$, which is itself a function of
$h_t$ rather than a constant. A Gaussian log density has curvature equal to minus
the reciprocal of its variance everywhere, a fixed number; here the curvature
vanishes as $h_t \to \infty$ and grows without bound as $h_t \to -\infty$, so no
single Gaussian matches $\ell$ at every point, which is what "not quadratic" means
concretely.

Contrast this with the state equation. Writing $h_t = \alpha + \phi h_{t-1} +
\sigma_h\zeta_t$ with $\alpha = \mu(1-\phi)$, the two transition densities linking
$h_t$ to its neighbours have log kernels $-(h_t-\alpha-\phi h_{t-1})^2/(2\sigma_h^2)$
and $-(h_{t+1}-\alpha-\phi h_t)^2/(2\sigma_h^2)$, each exactly quadratic in $h_t$
with constant curvature $-1/\sigma_h^2$ and $-\phi^2/\sigma_h^2$. Two quadratics
add to a quadratic, so the two transition densities alone multiply to a Gaussian in
$h_t$. It is only the measurement density that refuses to cooperate, and it is
exactly this piece that a Kalman update would need to fold in.
:::

The result is not an artefact of one model. The moment $r_t$ enters the return
equation through a random variance rather than a random mean, every model with that
feature loses the Kalman filter, because a random scale rather than a random shift
is what makes the measurement density non-Gaussian in the state. The chunk below
makes the shape concrete for the actual returns of this chapter, illustrating a
single state's target density under a stand-in Gaussian belief about its
neighbours, $h_t \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, 1)$ with $m_0$ set to twice the log of the
sample's daily standard deviation, at three representative absolute return sizes:
a typical day, a large day and an extreme day.

```{python}
m0 = 2 * np.log(r.std(ddof=1))
h_grid = np.linspace(m0 - 6, m0 + 6, 4000)
r_levels = {"typical day, median |r|": np.median(np.abs(r)),
            "large day, 90th pct |r|": np.quantile(np.abs(r), 0.90),
            "extreme day, 99th pct |r|": np.quantile(np.abs(r), 0.99)}

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
summary = []
for (lbl, rv), col in zip(r_levels.items(), ["C0", "C1", "C3"]):
    log_kernel = -h_grid / 2 - rv**2 * np.exp(-h_grid) / 2 - (h_grid - m0) ** 2 / 2
    dens = np.exp(log_kernel - log_kernel.max())
    dens /= np.trapezoid(dens, h_grid)
    mean = np.trapezoid(dens * h_grid, h_grid)
    var = np.trapezoid(dens * (h_grid - mean) ** 2, h_grid)
    skew = np.trapezoid(dens * (h_grid - mean) ** 3, h_grid) / var ** 1.5
    summary.append((lbl, rv, var, skew))
    ax.plot(h_grid, dens, color=col, label=f"{lbl} (|r| = {rv:.4f})")
ax.axvline(m0, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1, label="stand-in neighbour belief")
ax.set_xlabel("log variance $h_t$"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.set_title("One day's evidence reshapes belief about today's variance")
ax.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for lbl, rv, var, skew in summary:
    print(f"{lbl}: variance {var:.3f}, skewness {skew:+.3f}")
```

The three curves are the same neighbour belief updated by three different single
observations, and none of them is symmetric. On a typical day the update barely
tilts the density, leaving a skewness of $0.121$; on a large day the skewness rises
to $0.294$ and the spread narrows from a variance of $0.856$ to $0.556$, because a
big move is informative about variance and the neighbour belief no longer dominates;
on the most extreme day in the tails of the sample the skewness reaches $0.354$ and
the variance falls to $0.370$. A single return sharpens belief about that day's
variance and skews it to the right in log terms, exactly the asymmetry a Gaussian
cannot produce and exactly what R-12.1 predicts.

## Methodology: an exact sampler for an intractable path {#sec-methodology}

The repair is to stop pretending the integral in R-12.1 can be evaluated and
instead sample the joint posterior of the path and the parameters directly, block
by block, in the Metropolis-within-Gibbs spirit of Lecture 5. Because the state
equation is a first-order Markov chain, the full conditional of a single date
depends only on its two neighbours and the return observed that day, which is
enough local structure to build an exact sampler even though the joint likelihood
has none.

### Result R-12.2: the full conditional of a single log-volatility

The full conditional of an interior date factorises as

$$
p(h_t \mid h_{t-1}, h_{t+1}, r_t, \theta)
\;\propto\; p(r_t \mid h_t)\, p(h_t \mid h_{t-1})\, p(h_{t+1} \mid h_t),
$$

and the two transition factors alone multiply to a Gaussian with

$$
h_t^\ast = \frac{\alpha(1-\phi) + \phi\,(h_{t-1}+h_{t+1})}{1+\phi^2},
\qquad
v_t^\ast = \frac{\sigma_h^2}{1+\phi^2},
$$

with $\alpha = \mu(1-\phi)$, and the simplified means $\alpha + \phi h_{T-1}$ with
variance $\sigma_h^2$ at $t=T$, and $\mu(1-\phi)+\phi h_2$ with the same variance at
$t=1$, using the stationary prior in place of a missing predecessor. Proposing a
candidate from this Gaussian and correcting with a Metropolis step makes the
transition factors cancel out of the acceptance ratio, which collapses to the
measurement likelihood ratio alone,

$$
\log \alpha_{\text{MH}}
= -\tfrac12\big(h_t^{\text{new}} - h_t^{\text{old}}\big)
- \tfrac12\, r_t^2\Big(e^{-h_t^{\text{new}}} - e^{-h_t^{\text{old}}}\Big),
$$

truncated above at zero. Because the conditional of $h_t$ involves only its
neighbours, states at odd dates are conditionally independent given the states at
even dates, so an entire half of the path can be updated in one vectorised sweep.

R-12.2 is the general statement that makes single-move sampling possible at all.
It says nothing yet about how good the Gaussian proposal is as a stand-in for the
true, non-Gaussian target, only that whatever gap remains is entirely repaired by
the acceptance step; a poor proposal shows up as a low acceptance rate rather than
as a wrong answer. Jacquier, Polson and Rossi refine the proposal itself so that
the gap the Metropolis step has to repair is small even when a return is extreme,
which is the content of R-12.3.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: completing the square, and why the acceptance ratio collapses

Expanding the two transition log kernels in $h_t$, $-(h_t-\alpha-\phi h_{t-1})^2 -
(h_{t+1}-\alpha-\phi h_t)^2$, all divided by $2\sigma_h^2$, and collecting the
quadratic and linear terms in $h_t$ gives a Gaussian with precision
$(1+\phi^2)/\sigma_h^2$ and mean solving
$(1+\phi^2)h_t^\ast/\sigma_h^2 = \big[\alpha(1-\phi)+\phi(h_{t-1}+h_{t+1})\big]/\sigma_h^2$,
which is the displayed $h_t^\ast$ and $v_t^\ast$. At $t=T$ only the incoming
transition applies, giving mean $\alpha+\phi h_{T-1}$ and variance $\sigma_h^2$
directly; at $t=1$ the stationary initial density
$h_1 \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu, \sigma_h^2/(1-\phi^2)\big)$ plays the role of the
missing predecessor and combines with the one transition to $h_2$ in the same way.

For the acceptance ratio, write the full target as $p(r_t\mid h_t)\,g(h_t)$ with
$g$ the Gaussian just derived, and propose $h_t^{\text{new}} \sim g$. The
Metropolis acceptance probability for an independence proposal is
$\min\{1, [\pi(h^{\text{new}})q(h^{\text{old}})] / [\pi(h^{\text{old}})q(h^{\text{new}})]\}$
with $\pi = p(r_t\mid h_t)g(h_t)$ and $q=g$; the two factors of $g$ appear once in
the numerator and once in the denominator and cancel exactly, leaving the ratio of
$p(r_t\mid h_t)$ alone, which is the displayed $\log\alpha_{\text{MH}}$.
:::

### Result R-12.3: an accept-reject construction that samples the exact conditional, and the parameter blocks that complete the sweep

Working instead with the variance scale $s_t = e^{h_t}$, its conditional density
with respect to $\mathrm{d}s_t$ has kernel
$s_t^{-3/2}\exp\big[-r_t^2/(2s_t) - (\log s_t - m_t)^2/(2v_t)\big]$, the same target
as R-12.2 with a Jacobian attached and $m_t, v_t$ standing for $h_t^\ast, v_t^\ast$.
Matching the mean and variance of a $\text{Lognormal}(m_t,v_t)$ to an inverse gamma
gives a blanket $q = \text{IG}(a_L, b_L)$ with
$a_L = 2 + 1/(e^{v_t}-1)$ and $b_L = (a_L-1)e^{m_t+v_t/2}$, and multiplying that
blanket by the return kernel gives the tractable proposal
$q' = \text{IG}(a_L + \tfrac12,\, b_L + r_t^2/2)$. An accept-reject step against
$cq'$ followed by one further Metropolis correction draws exactly from the target
for any finite $c$, matched here at the mode of the target rather than as a strict
upper bound, because the Metropolis correction repairs whatever the accept-reject
step leaves imperfect. This is the construction due to Jacquier, Polson and Rossi,
and it is what makes single-move sampling of a whole eighteen-year path practical
rather than merely correct in principle.

The path is only half of the unknowns. Writing the state equation as a regression,
$h_t = \alpha + \phi h_{t-1} + \sigma_h\zeta_t$, puts $(\alpha,\phi)$ in exactly the
Normal linear regression setting of Lecture 2, and $\sigma_h^2$ follows the same
inverse-gamma conditional, once the stationary initial state is added as one extra
observation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: the moment-matched blanket, and the state-equation conjugate updates

Since a lognormal has relative variance $e^{v_t}-1$ while an inverse gamma
$\text{IG}(a,b)$ has relative variance $1/(a-2)$, setting them equal gives
$a_L = 2+1/(e^{v_t}-1)$; matching means, $b_L/(a_L-1) = e^{m_t+v_t/2}$, gives the
displayed $b_L$. Multiplying the return kernel $s_t^{-1}\exp(-r_t^2/(2s_t))$, which
is itself proportional to an $\text{IG}(1/2, r_t^2/2)$ kernel with respect to
$\mathrm{d}s_t$, by the blanket $q$ gives a product of two inverse-gamma kernels in
the same variable, which is again inverse gamma with shapes and scales added,
$q' = \text{IG}(a_L+\tfrac12,\, b_L+r_t^2/2)$. The accept-reject step retains a
candidate from $q'$ with probability $\min\{1, p(s)/(cq'(s))\}$; its output has
density proportional to $f(s)=\min\{p(s), cq'(s)\}$, which need not equal $p$
itself, so a further independence Metropolis step with ratio $p(s')f(s)/(p(s)f(s'))$
removes whatever discrepancy $f$ still carries, and the two steps together are
exact regardless of how $c$ is chosen, provided $c>0$.

For the parameter blocks, stack $Z = [\mathbf{1}, h_{1:T-1}]$ and $y = h_{2:T}$,
give $\gamma=(\alpha,\phi)$ a Normal prior $\mathcal{N}(g_0, G_0)$ truncated to
$|\phi|<1$, and complete the square exactly as in Lecture 2 to get the Gaussian
posterior $\gamma \mid \sigma_h^2, h \sim \mathcal{N}(g_1, G_1)$ with
$G_1 = (G_0^{-1}+Z^\top Z/\sigma_h^2)^{-1}$ and
$g_1 = G_1(G_0^{-1}g_0 + Z^\top y/\sigma_h^2)$; because the truncation and the
stationary initial-state density $h_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha/(1-\phi),
\sigma_h^2/(1-\phi^2))$ are not part of the Normal-regression likelihood, a
candidate drawn from this Gaussian is accepted with an extra Metropolis step whose
ratio is the ratio of the two candidates' stationary initial-state densities alone,
since everything else cancels. Finally
$\sigma_h^2 \mid \gamma, h \sim \text{IG}\big(c_0+T/2,\, d_0 + \tfrac12[\lVert
y-Z\gamma\rVert^2 + (1-\phi^2)(h_1-\alpha/(1-\phi))^2]\big)$, the usual
inverse-gamma update with one extra quadratic term contributed by the initial
state, so that every block conditions on the same stationary starting density
rather than only some of them.
:::

Together R-12.2 and R-12.3 turn an intractable integral into a sequence of exact,
cheap draws: a Gaussian-proposal Metropolis step for the bulk of the path, an
accept-reject and Metropolis construction for the full non-Gaussian conditional
when precision matters, and a Normal-Inverse-Gamma block for the parameters that
govern persistence and the scale of volatility shocks. What the sampler cannot fix
is how slowly it explores a highly persistent path, and that is a cost paid in
computation rather than in correctness, as the empirical section shows directly.

## Data: the daily excess return on the US market, 2005-2022 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the daily Fama-French factor file,
`data/ff_factors_daily.parquet`, and the single series used anywhere in this
chapter is the excess return on the US market portfolio. The window, January 2005
to December 2022, is chosen so that the sample contains more than one crisis rather
than one: the financial crisis of 2008 and 2009, the flash crash of May 2010, the
euro area and downgrade turmoil of August 2011, the pandemic crash of March 2020
and the inflation and rate shock of 2022. Eighteen years is also short enough that
the whole sampler, path and parameters together, runs in about ten seconds, so
nothing in this chapter needs subsampling or a shortened chain. The series is
demeaned before use, since the model has no intercept in its measurement equation
and leaving one in would push the mean into the volatility state.

```{python}
#| label: fig-market-returns
#| fig-cap: "Daily US market excess return, January 2005 to December 2022, with the single worst and best day marked."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
ax.plot(dates, r, lw=0.4, color="grey")
i_min, i_max = int(r.argmin()), int(r.argmax())
ax.plot(dates[i_min], r[i_min], "o", color="firebrick", ms=5)
ax.plot(dates[i_max], r[i_max], "o", color="seagreen", ms=5)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("daily excess return")
ax.set_title("The single dataset used throughout this chapter")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{T} trading days, {dates[0]:%Y-%m-%d} to {dates[-1]:%Y-%m-%d}")
print(f"mean daily excess return removed {window['mkt_rf'].mean():.6f}")
print(f"standard deviation {r.std(ddof=1):.6f} ({r.std(ddof=1)*np.sqrt(252):.2%} annualised)")
print(f"excess kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r):.2f}, skewness {stats.skew(r):+.3f}")
print(f"worst day {r.min():.4f} on {dates[i_min]:%Y-%m-%d}, "
      f"best day {r.max():.4f} on {dates[i_max]:%Y-%m-%d}")
```

The sample is $4{,}531$ trading days. Its unconditional standard deviation is
$1.257\%$ a day, an annualised $19.95\%$, and its excess kurtosis is $11.14$ with a
skewness of $-0.314$, both far from the zero a Gaussian return would deliver. The
worst day is $-12.05\%$ on 16 March 2020, marked in red, and the best is $11.32\%$
on 13 October 2008, marked in green, and it is not a coincidence that the two
largest moves of either sign sit inside the two largest crises: fat tails and
volatility clustering are two descriptions of the same phenomenon, which is
precisely what the stochastic-volatility model is built to connect.

## Empirical analysis: fitting the model to eighteen years of daily returns {#sec-empirical}

```{python}
from scipy.special import gammaln

def log_variance_target(log_s, r2, mean, variance):
    """Conditional variance density evaluated at log(s), with respect to ds."""
    return -1.5*log_s-r2*np.exp(-log_s)/2-(log_s-mean)**2/(2*variance)

def log_ig_at_log(log_s, shape, scale):
    """Inverse-Gamma log density with respect to ds, evaluated at log(s)."""
    return shape*np.log(scale)-gammaln(shape)-(shape+1)*log_s-scale*np.exp(-log_s)

def jpr_update(old, r2, mean, variance, rng):
    """JPR accept-reject/MH update using a moment-matched inverse-Gamma blanket."""
    a_ln = 2+1/np.expm1(variance)
    b_ln = (a_ln-1)*np.exp(mean+variance/2)
    shape, scale = a_ln+.5, b_ln+r2/2
    log_c = (log_variance_target(mean,r2,mean,variance)
             -log_ig_at_log(mean,shape,scale))
    proposal = old.copy()
    pending = np.arange(len(old))
    while len(pending):
        candidate = -np.log(rng.gamma(shape[pending],1/scale[pending]))
        lp = log_variance_target(candidate,r2[pending],mean[pending],variance[pending])
        lq = log_ig_at_log(candidate,shape[pending],scale[pending])
        keep = np.log(rng.random(len(pending))) < np.minimum(0,lp-log_c[pending]-lq)
        proposal[pending[keep]] = candidate[keep]
        pending = pending[~keep]
    old_p = log_variance_target(old,r2,mean,variance)
    new_p = log_variance_target(proposal,r2,mean,variance)
    old_f = np.minimum(old_p,log_c+log_ig_at_log(old,shape,scale))
    new_f = np.minimum(new_p,log_c+log_ig_at_log(proposal,shape,scale))
    accept = np.log(rng.random(len(old))) < new_p-old_p+old_f-new_f
    return np.where(accept,proposal,old), int(accept.sum())

def initial_log_density(h0, alpha, phi, s2):
    """Stationary initial-state density, omitting a parameter-independent constant."""
    return float(.5*np.log(1-phi**2)-.5*np.log(s2)
                 -(1-phi**2)*(h0-alpha/(1-phi))**2/(2*s2))

g0, G0 = np.array([0.0, 0.9]), np.diag([10.0, 0.25])
G0_inv = np.linalg.inv(G0)
c0, d0 = 6.0, 0.20                       # prior mean of sigma_h^2 equals 0.04
n_iter, burn = 10_000, 3000
h, phi, s2 = np.full(T, np.log(r.var())), 0.9, 0.05
alpha = np.log(r.var()) * (1 - phi)
even, odd, r2 = np.arange(0, T, 2), np.arange(1, T, 2), r**2
par_draws, h_draws = np.empty((n_iter - burn, 3)), np.empty((n_iter - burn, T))
acc = n_prop = 0

for it in range(n_iter):
    mu = alpha / (1 - phi)
    for grp in (even, odd):              # two conditionally independent half-sweeps
        m, v = np.empty(T), np.full(T, s2)
        m[1:-1] = (alpha * (1 - phi) + phi * (h[:-2] + h[2:])) / (1 + phi**2)
        v[1:-1] = s2 / (1 + phi**2)
        m[0], m[-1] = mu * (1 - phi) + phi * h[1], alpha + phi * h[-2]
        h[grp], accepted = jpr_update(h[grp], r2[grp], m[grp], v[grp], rng)
        acc += accepted
        n_prop += grp.size
    Z, y = np.column_stack([np.ones(T - 1), h[:-1]]), h[1:]
    G1 = np.linalg.inv(G0_inv + Z.T @ Z / s2)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(G1)
    g1 = G1 @ (G0_inv @ g0 + Z.T @ y / s2)
    cand = g1 + L @ rng.standard_normal(2)
    while abs(cand[1]) >= 1:
        cand = g1 + L @ rng.standard_normal(2)
    log_ratio = (initial_log_density(h[0], cand[0], cand[1], s2)
                 - initial_log_density(h[0], alpha, phi, s2))
    if np.log(rng.random()) < log_ratio:
        alpha, phi = cand
    e = y - Z @ np.array([alpha, phi])
    initial_ss = (1-phi**2)*(h[0]-alpha/(1-phi))**2
    s2 = 1.0 / rng.gamma(c0 + T/2, 1.0 / (d0 + 0.5*(e @ e + initial_ss)))
    if it >= burn:
        par_draws[it - burn] = [alpha / (1 - phi), phi, np.sqrt(s2)]
        h_draws[it - burn] = h

print(f"kept {par_draws.shape[0]} draws, acceptance rate {acc / n_prop:.3f}")
```

Seven thousand draws are kept after a burn-in of three thousand, and the reported
acceptance rate concerns only the final Metropolis correction; the accept-reject
step inside it also carries a computational cost, and neither a high rate nor a
completed run by itself establishes good mixing, which the trace below checks
directly.

```{python}
def inefficiency(x, lag_max=250):
    z = x - x.mean()
    ac = np.correlate(z, z, "full")[len(z) - 1:] / (len(z) * z.var())
    return 1.0 + 2.0 * ac[1:lag_max + 1].sum()

q = np.quantile(par_draws, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
print(pd.DataFrame({
    "post mean": par_draws.mean(axis=0),
    "5%": q[0], "95%": q[1],
    "inefficiency": [inefficiency(par_draws[:, j]) for j in range(3)],
}, index=["mu", "phi", "sigma_h"]).round(4))

phi_hat, sig_hat, mu_hat = par_draws[:, 1].mean(), par_draws[:, 2].mean(), par_draws[:, 0].mean()
print(f"half-life of a volatility shock: {np.log(0.5)/np.log(phi_hat):.1f} days")
print(f"annualised volatility at the long-run level: {np.exp(mu_hat/2)*np.sqrt(252):.2%}")
```

Persistence has posterior mean $0.9773$ with a ninety percent credible interval
from $0.9707$ to $0.9836$, comfortably below the unit root that would make
volatility shocks permanent. Read as a half-life, a shock to log variance decays by
half in $30.2$ days, about six trading weeks, which is why a crisis that is over in
the news is not over in a risk model. The volatility of volatility has posterior
mean $0.2255$, and the long-run level $\mu$ corresponds to an annualised volatility
of $13.93\%$, below the unconditional $19.95\%$ of the whole window because the log
scale means the average log variance sits below the log of the average variance.
The inefficiency factors, well above one for every parameter, are the warning
attached to all of this: a sampler that shifts one date at a time moves through the
posterior's dependence slowly, so seven thousand nominal draws deliver far fewer
effectively independent ones, an effective sample size of about $2{,}750$ for
$\mu$ but only around $55$ for the far more persistent $\sigma_h$. Combining the
two estimated parameters gives a stationary standard deviation of the log variance
of $\sigma_h/\sqrt{1-\phi^2} = 1.065$, which is the sense in which volatility
varies over an enormous range in this model: plus or minus two of those is a
factor of $e^{2\times 1.065}\approx 8.4$ in variance, entirely from the state
equation and before any single day's return is even observed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-param-histograms
#| fig-cap: "Marginal posteriors of persistence and volatility of volatility, from the same retained draws as the summary table."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axL.hist(par_draws[:, 1], bins=40, density=True, color="C1", alpha=0.75)
axL.set_xlabel(r"$\phi$"); axL.set_ylabel("posterior density"); axL.set_title("Persistence")
axR.hist(par_draws[:, 2], bins=40, density=True, color="C0", alpha=0.75)
axR.set_xlabel(r"$\sigma_h$"); axR.set_title("Volatility of volatility")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Persistence is left-skewed with a long tail towards lower values and a hard
economic ceiling at one, while the volatility of volatility is mildly right-skewed;
neither marginal is well described by its mean alone, which is the first reason to
report intervals rather than point estimates. The two shapes are a visible
signature of R-12.2 and R-12.3 at work: $\phi$ is pinned down by how the path as a
whole moves from date to date, a quantity the accept-reject construction estimates
only through many correlated single-date draws, while $\sigma_h$ is pinned down by
the size of those moves and inherits the same dependence, so both histograms are
smoother summaries of a chain that itself mixes slowly, which the next figure
shows directly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-trace-phi
#| fig-cap: "Retained draws of persistence together with their running mean, showing how slowly the chain settles."
phi_chain = par_draws[:, 1]
running_mean_phi = np.cumsum(phi_chain) / np.arange(1, len(phi_chain) + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(phi_chain, color="C1", lw=0.4, alpha=0.6, label="retained draws of phi")
ax.plot(running_mean_phi, color="black", lw=1.5, label="running mean")
ax.set_xlabel("retained iteration"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\phi$")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Persistence draws mix slowly")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The running mean keeps drifting well into the chain rather than flattening out
after a few hundred iterations, visual confirmation of the inefficiency factor
printed above: consecutive draws of $\phi$ carry much less information than
consecutive independent draws would, which is the price paid for a sampler that
moves the path one date at a time. None of this calls the answer into question,
since the reported credible interval already accounts for the dependence through
the inefficiency-adjusted standard error, but it is the reason ten thousand
iterations rather than one thousand were budgeted at the start of this section,
and it is exactly the cost the mixture sampler of the exercise session trades away
by drawing the whole path in one block instead of one date at a time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-vol-path
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean annualised volatility with a 90% credible band, market excess returns 2005-2022. The six marked points are local peaks at least 90 trading days apart."
ann = np.sqrt(252)
vol_draws = ann * np.exp(h_draws / 2)
vol_mean = vol_draws.mean(axis=0)
vol_lo, vol_hi = np.quantile(vol_draws, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)

available = np.ones(T, bool)
peaks = []
for i in np.argsort(-vol_mean):
    if len(peaks) == 6:
        break
    if available[i]:
        peaks.append(i)
        available[max(0, i - 90):i + 90] = False
peaks = sorted(peaks)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
ax.fill_between(dates, vol_lo, vol_hi, color="C0", alpha=0.25, label="90% credible band")
ax.plot(dates, vol_mean, color="C0", lw=1.0, label="posterior mean")
ax.plot(dates[peaks], vol_mean[peaks], "o", color="black", ms=5)
for i in peaks:
    ax.annotate(f"{dates[i]:%b %Y}", (dates[i], vol_mean[i]),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4, 7), fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("annualised volatility")
ax.set_title("Posterior stochastic volatility of the US market, 2005-2022")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"calmest day {dates[vol_mean.argmin()]:%Y-%m-%d} at {vol_mean.min():.2%}, "
      f"most turbulent {dates[vol_mean.argmax()]:%Y-%m-%d} at {vol_mean.max():.2%}")
print(f"width of the band on the most turbulent day: "
      f"[{vol_lo[vol_mean.argmax()]:.2%}, {vol_hi[vol_mean.argmax()]:.2%}]")
```

The six marked peaks are a list of the last two decades of financial history, and
the sampler was never told any of the dates: 16 March 2020, the Monday the Federal
Reserve cut to zero after the pandemic was declared; 13 October 2008, a month after
Lehman Brothers failed; and four more that any market historian would recognise on
sight. The calmest day of the whole eighteen years reaches only $4.63\%$ annualised
while the most turbulent reaches $92.97\%$, a factor of twenty that a model with a
single $\sigma$ cannot represent. The band is wide and widest exactly where
volatility is high, because the log scale makes uncertainty multiplicative: on the
worst day it runs from $70.7\%$ to $121.9\%$, so even at the peak of a crisis the
model declines to say whether volatility was seventy percent or a hundred and
twenty. That width is intrinsic rather than a defect of the sampler, since a single
squared return is a noisy $\chi^2_1$ signal about the variance that produced it,
and no amount of extra iterations narrows it, because the uncertainty is about the
world rather than about the chain. Each draw underlying this figure conditions on
the entire eighteen-year sample, so the path shown is smoothed rather than
filtered: the estimate on a given day already uses returns that came after it as
well as before, which is the right object for describing history and the wrong one
for a forecast made in real time, a distinction the next chapter returns to.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ewma-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Three volatility measures on the same returns: a model-free centred realised measure, the industry-standard exponentially weighted average, and the posterior mean of the stochastic-volatility model."
lam = 0.94
ewma_var = np.empty(T)
ewma_var[0] = r[:50].var()
for t in range(1, T):
    ewma_var[t] = lam * ewma_var[t - 1] + (1 - lam) * r[t - 1] ** 2
ewma_vol = ann * np.sqrt(ewma_var)

realised = ann * (pd.Series(r).rolling(11, center=True, min_periods=11)
                  .apply(lambda z: np.sqrt((z ** 2).mean()), raw=True).to_numpy())
ok = ~np.isnan(realised)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
ax.plot(dates, realised, color="grey", lw=0.8, label="centred 11-day realised volatility")
ax.plot(dates, ewma_vol, color="C3", lw=0.9, label="EWMA, $\\lambda = 0.94$")
ax.plot(dates, vol_mean, color="C0", lw=1.1, label="stochastic volatility, posterior mean")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("annualised volatility (log scale)")
ax.set_title("Three volatility measures on the same returns")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for name, v in (("stochastic volatility", vol_mean), ("EWMA(0.94)", ewma_vol)):
    print(f"{name:22s} correlation with realised {np.corrcoef(v[ok], realised[ok])[0, 1]:.4f}   "
          f"log RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log(v[ok])-np.log(realised[ok]))**2)):.4f}")
print(f"share of days EWMA lies inside the 90% credible band: "
      f"{np.mean((ewma_vol >= vol_lo) & (ewma_vol <= vol_hi)):.4f}")
```

Against the centred realised measure the stochastic-volatility path has a
correlation of $0.9757$ and a log root mean squared error of $0.1691$, while the
exponentially weighted average manages $0.8437$ and $0.3326$, roughly twice as
large in log terms. The exponentially weighted line jumps the day after every
large return and then decays mechanically, so it lags at the start of each crisis
and overshoots on the way out, while the smoothed posterior path turns before the
peak because it is allowed to use both sides of the data. The two are rarely in
outright conflict, since the EWMA line lies inside the ninety percent credible band
on $86.2\%$ of days, but what the Bayesian treatment adds is not usually a
different number. It is an honest band on a crisis day nearly a factor of two wide,
where the EWMA line conceals that same uncertainty entirely; an estimated rather
than assumed decay, $\phi = 0.9773$ against the fixed convention $\lambda = 0.94$;
and mean reversion to $13.93\%$, which the exponentially weighted recursion has no
mechanism to produce at all, since a fixed $\lambda$ implies a random walk in
variance with no pull back towards any long-run level. The price for all of this
is computational rather than conceptual: the exponentially weighted average is one
line of arithmetic evaluated once, while the posterior path took a ten-thousand
iteration sampler whose inefficiency factors were printed two figures ago, and a
risk desk choosing between the two is choosing between a convention that costs
nothing and a measurement that costs ten seconds and reports its own uncertainty.

## Discussion: what the path buys, and the limit of a single volatility state {#sec-discussion}

```{python}
#| label: fig-fat-tails
#| fig-cap: "Standardised market returns against a Gaussian benchmark, on a log density scale so the tails are visible."
r_std = (r - r.mean()) / r.std()
grid_r = np.linspace(-10, 10, 400)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(r_std, bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.6, color="C0",
        label="market excess returns (standardised)")
ax.plot(grid_r, stats.norm.pdf(grid_r), color="black", lw=1.5, label="Gaussian benchmark")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("standardised return"); ax.set_ylabel("density (log scale)")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Stochastic volatility generates fat tails from Gaussian shocks")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

kurt_model = 3 * np.exp(sig_hat ** 2 / (1 - phi_hat ** 2)) - 3
print(f"excess kurtosis: sample {stats.kurtosis(r):.2f}, "
      f"model-implied 3*exp(sigma_h^2/(1-phi^2))-3 = {kurt_model:.2f}")
print(f"posterior correlation of phi and sigma_h: "
      f"{np.corrcoef(par_draws[:, 1], par_draws[:, 2])[0, 1]:.3f}")
```

The check against something already known is the fat tails documented since
Lecture 4 asked what a Student-t error buys over a Normal one. Every shock in this
model, $u_t$ and $\zeta_t$, is Gaussian, yet the histogram sits visibly above the
Gaussian curve away from the centre. The sample excess kurtosis is $11.14$ and the
value implied by the posterior means of $\phi$ and $\sigma_h$ is $6.33$: both are
far above the Gaussian benchmark of zero, so a randomly moving variance is clearly
the right mechanism, though it accounts for only part of the observed tail
thickness, the remainder being a handful of crash days a fourth moment estimates
very imprecisely. Fat tails here are not an add-on but a direct, quantifiable
consequence of letting the variance itself be random, exactly the connection the
Overview promised.

The limitation is a posterior correlation of $-0.565$ between $\phi$ and
$\sigma_h$: the data speak mainly to their product, the stationary variance
$\sigma_h^2/(1-\phi^2)$, and much less to the two ingredients separately, so a
jagged path with high $\sigma_h$ and low $\phi$ and a smooth path with low
$\sigma_h$ and high $\phi$ can generate return series that are nearly
indistinguishable. Eighteen years of daily data is already a long sample, and the
identification is still loose, which is the reason the credible intervals on
$\phi$ reported earlier matter as much as the point estimate.

What the whole exercise delivers is a path and two interpretable parameters where
the industry default delivers one line and a convention. What it still assumes is
that risk is the only thing a portfolio needs to know about the return
distribution, and that estimating that risk is the hard part. Lecture 13 keeps
this same idea, a predictive distribution rather than a plug-in estimate, and asks
the harder question a risk desk actually faces: not how volatile an asset is, but
how much of it to hold, once the uncertainty in both the mean and the variance is
taken seriously.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 12 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/12-stochastic-volatility.qmd) works through them and
adds the lab.

1. By hand. Starting from the two transition densities in R-12.2, complete the
   square to rederive $h_t^\ast$ and $v_t^\ast$ for an interior date, and then
   redo the calculation for $t=1$ using the stationary initial density in place of
   a missing predecessor. Confirm that the acceptance ratio of R-12.2 depends only
   on $r_t$ and not on $h_{t-1}$ or $h_{t+1}$.

2. Computational. Refit the sampler of @sec-empirical with the prior mean of
   $\sigma_h^2$ doubled and halved in turn, holding $c_0$ fixed, and report how the
   posterior mean and interval of $\phi$ and $\sigma_h$ move. Then compute the
   inefficiency factor of the path itself, at three representative dates, one in a
   calm period and two in different crises, and relate the differences to the
   local persistence of the path.

3. On real data. Refit the model on the daily excess return of a single industry
   portfolio from the same file rather than the market, over the same window, and
   compare its estimated persistence, volatility of volatility and long-run level
   with the market's. Report whether the industry's volatility peaks fall on the
   same dates as the market's, and whether its posterior correlation between
   $\phi$ and $\sigma_h$ is as strong as the one found here.

Exercise 1 is worth doing before the session, since the same completing-the-square
step reappears with a more elaborate accept-reject construction in R-12.3.
Exercises 2 and 3 reuse the code of @sec-empirical with the prior or the input
series changed, and the exercise session also works through the Kim, Shephard and
Chib mixture sampler as an alternative to the single-move construction used here.

## Reading and references

The Metropolis-within-Gibbs logic follows Geweke (2005), Section 4.6.2. The single-
move sampler of R-12.2 and R-12.3, the moment-matched inverse-gamma blanket and the
stationary initial-state correction all follow Jacquier, Polson and Rossi (1994);
this material is not covered directly by the UPM examples used elsewhere in the
course. The mixture-of-normals alternative due to Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998),
which restores linearity by approximating the log-chi-squared observation error
with a fixed mixture of normals, is taken up in the Week 12 exercise session rather
than here, together with the two-state Bayesian illustration behind the Overview's
opening intuition.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Jacquier, Polson, and Rossi (1994), "Bayesian Analysis of Stochastic Volatility
Models," *Journal of Business and Economic Statistics*. Kim, Shephard, and Chib
(1998), "Stochastic Volatility: Likelihood Inference and Comparison with ARCH
Models," *Review of Economic Studies*. Chan, Koop, Poirier, and Tobias, *Bayesian
Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. on state-space models and stochastic
volatility. Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 8.
